summary: CERC has proposed that pumped storage plants (PSPs) be allowed to sell in the High Price Day Ahead Market (HP-DAM), which is currently open only to gas stations using imported RLNG or naphtha, imported-coal stations and battery storage. The proposal follows NLDC recommendations of July 2026 and a Ministry of Power letter of 30.07.2026. NLDC's analysis noted that operational PSP capacity (7,425.6 MW) is largely tied up, and that HP-DAM cleared on only 47 days between April 2025 and July 2026. It also found a solar-hour to evening-peak price spread in the DAM of about ₹4.37 per unit. The Commission took the prima facie view that the DAM alone may not give PSPs enough opportunity and that HP-DAM access could improve their viability and support grid flexibility. This is a proposal, not a final order: CERC has started suo motu proceedings, issued a public notice, and asked parties to file written submissions within 15 days of the order dated 28.10.2026.

summary: CERC has rejected Vena Energy's plea to treat its 160 MW blended wind project in Koppal, Karnataka (129.6 MW wind, 30.4 MW solar) as a wind generator for deviation settlement. The project was bid under MNRE's 2020 Blended Wind Guidelines and commissioned on 29.10.2024. SRPC treats it as a hybrid because it has wind and solar behind one injection point, which puts it in the tighter deviation band for solar and hybrid sellers under Regulation 8(4) of the DSM Regulations, 2024. Vena said this raised its DSM liability to about 5.3% of revenue, against about 3.0% if treated as wind. The Commission held that qualifying under the Blended Wind Guidelines does not decide treatment under the DSM Regulations. The 33% hybrid threshold in other guidelines is not relevant either, and the developer could have built a wind-only project, as another bidder in the same tranche did. Crucially, the Commission said its powers to relax and remove difficulty under Regulations 11 and 12 cannot be used to create a new category of generating station.

summary: RERC has dismissed Shree Cement's petition under Section 142 against JVVNL. Shree Cement's Jobner grinding unit has a contract demand of 7.40 MVA and a 7.08 MW behind-the-meter captive solar plant commissioned in March 2023. It asked JVVNL to reduce its contract demand to 3,540 kVA and add BESS, relying on the fourth and fifth provisos to Regulation 5(ii) of the RERC (Terms and Conditions for Green Energy Open Access) Regulations, 2025, which allow captive RE capacity up to 200% of contract demand with BESS for energy from capacity above 100%. JVVNL refused. The Commission held that the GEOA Regulations deal expressly with existing plants through the one-time conversion option in Regulation 7, so the saving clause in Regulation 31 cannot be used to bring in the 200% limit for a plant that stays under the earlier regime, where captive capacity was capped at 100% of contract demand. Read with its object, the enhanced limit is meant to encourage additional RE capacity, not to let a consumer reduce contract demand and fixed charges with no new capacity. RERC agreed that, on a plain reading, the provisos limit a behind-the-meter plant to contract demand, and noted that the petitioner had made the same suggestion in the GEOA procedure hearings (order of 12.12.2025) without disclosing it.

summary: NHPC Limited asked the Commission to adopt, under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003, the tariff for 1,150 MW of additional firm and despatchable renewable power with energy storage. NHPC had allocated this capacity under a "Greenshoe Option" at the lowest auction tariff of Rs 4.48/kWh. The Commission adopted tariffs for the 1,200 MW base capacity on 19.06.2025 in Petition No. 87/AT/2025. When it later dismissed NHPC's review petition, it allowed a fresh petition for the Greenshoe quantity. The Commission noted that the Central Government's bidding guidelines do not define or expressly provide for a "Greenshoe Option". It said such allocation might raise concerns about transparency and equal treatment of bidders. It expects implementing agencies not to use the option in future without an express provision in the guidelines. Treating this as a legacy case, it adopted the tariffs. It restricted Juniper Green Energy's Greenshoe allocation to 200 MW instead of 300 MW, giving 1,050 MW at Rs 4.48/kWh, subject to PSAs being signed with distribution licensees. A trading margin of Rs 0.07/kWh is deemed consistent with the Trading Licence Regulations if distribution licensees agree. Where the escrow or letter of credit is not provided, it is capped at Rs 0.02/kWh.
headline: CERC adopts Rs 4.48/kWh tariff for 1,050 MW of NHPC greenshoe storage-backed RE power

summary: Parighosh Realtors and Developers is developing a 200 MW wind-solar hybrid project in Kutch with connectivity at GETCO's 220 kV Bhachunda substation. GETCO demanded an Associated Transmission System Bank Guarantee (ATS BG) of Rs 20 lakh per MW, Rs 40 crore in total. The developer argued that the 220 kV switchyard and lines were commissioned in December 2020, the substation was state-planned under the Green Energy Corridor, and no new transmission was being built on its account. GETCO said there was no evacuation margin when the application was received, so it was put on hold. It was later processed under Clause 2.2 read with Clause 7.3 of the Connectivity Procedure, 2025, and provisional connectivity was granted on 15.11.2025, subject to system strengthening, with a tentative timeline of December 2027. The Commission held that the earlier commissioning of the 220 kV switchyard does not show that the 200 MW could be evacuated without strengthening. It found that Clause 7.3 covers provisional connectivity under Clauses 5.1(i) and 5.1(ii) and requires the ATS BG. It followed its decisions in Petition Nos. 2626 and 2634 of 2026 and found that GETCO's reliance on Clause 7.3 was not a new ground. The petition was rejected, and the developer must furnish the ATS BG.
headline: Gujarat developer must furnish Rs 40 crore transmission bank guarantee for 200 MW Bhachunda connectivity

summary: Shri Om Agro Products runs a 1.5 MW wind plant in Jaisalmer under a 2013 PPA-cum-wheeling and banking agreement. Under it, 50% of generation was sold to the Discom at Rs 4.89 per unit and 50% was kept for the firm's own captive use. summary: Shri Om Agro Products owns a 1.5 MW wind plant. In 2013 it signed a tripartite wheeling agreement with RVPN and Suzlon Energy covering 0.75 MW for captive use. An amended PPA dated 15.07.2024 moved that 0.75 MW to sale to the discom at Rs 2.44/kWh. RVPN then demanded Rs 15,86,864 in surrender charges under Regulation 14 of the RERC Open Access Regulations, 2016. When the petitioner did not pay, RVPN had the plant disconnected on 28.05.2025. The petitioner argued that these charges compensate only for stranded capacity, and that none existed because the discom now used the same transmission system. The Commission held that Regulation 14(2) sets the charges on a normative basis: 66% of transmission and wheeling charges, for at most three years. Actual stranded capacity therefore need not be shown, and the Commission added that it cannot be assessed with certainty in a meshed network. It read stranded capacity as relinquished capacity and held that the sale to the discom did not waive the liability. It had earlier ordered reconnection on deposit of 25% of the charges, and it now directed the petitioner to pay the balance. The order does not separately rule on the disconnection or the compensation claim.
